title: Ὀρνιθοθήρας καὶ κορύδαλος
part: The Fowler and the Lark (Chambry 283 · Perry 193)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 283 (= Perry 193). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A fowler was setting snares for birds.
sentences.n: The page prints Ὀρνιθορήρας, with a rho where the word wants a theta; every other occurrence in this fable and its neighbours reads ὀρνιθοθήρας, 'bird-hunter, fowler', so this is almost certainly a slip of the type-case rather than a reading. The form is kept as printed. ἵστη is the imperfect of ἵστημι — he was in the middle of setting them up. ὄρνις is the general word for a bird here; at fable 286 the same noun has to be read 'hen'.

sentences.t: Κορύδαλος δὲ τοῦτον πόρρωθεν ἰδὼν ἐπυνθάνετο τί ποτ’ ἐργάζοιτο.
sentences.tr: Korydalos de touton porrōthen idōn epynthaneto ti pot’ ergazoito.
sentences.l: And a lark, having seen him from a distance, asked what on earth he was doing.
sentences.n: ἐργάζοιτο is an optative in an indirect question after a main verb in past time — Greek regularly shifts the mood that way, and the optative marks the whole question as reported rather than asked. τί ποτε piles the emphasis onto the interrogative: 'what ever'. The κορύδαλος is the crested lark, a bird of open ground that would be working the same fields as the fowler.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ πόλιν κτίζειν φαμένου, εἶτα δὲ πορρωτέρω ἀποχωρήσαντος καὶ κρυβέντος, ὁ κορύδαλος τοῖς τοῦ ἀνδρὸς λόγοις πιστεύσας, προσελθὼν εἰς τὸν βρόχον ἑάλω.
sentences.tr: Tou de polin ktizein phamenou, eita de porrōterō apochōrēsantos kai krybentos, ho korydalos tois tou andros logois pisteusas, proselthōn eis ton brochon healō.
sentences.l: And when he said that he was founding a city, and then had withdrawn further off and hidden himself, the lark, having trusted the man's words, came up and was caught in the noose.
sentences.i: The fowler said that he was founding a city, and then withdrew further off and hid himself; and the lark, believing what he had said, came up and was caught in the noose.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute, this time carrying three participles in a row (φαμένου, ἀποχωρήσαντος, κρυβέντος) — the chain of participles is the ordinary engine of a fable's narrative. ἑάλω is the aorist of ἁλίσκομαι, 'be taken, be caught', which serves as the passive of αἱρέω.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ὀρνιθοθήρα ἐπιδραμόντος, ἐκεῖνος εἶπεν· « Ὦ οὗτος, εἰ τοιαύτην πόλιν κτίζεις, οὐ πολλοὺς εὑρήσεις τοὺς ἐνοικοῦντας. »
sentences.tr: Tou de ornithothēra epidramontos, ekeinos eipen· « Ō houtos, ei toiautēn polin ktizeis, ou pollous heurēseis tous enoikountas. »
sentences.l: And when the fowler ran up, that one said: « You there, if you are founding such a city as this, you will not find many to live in it. »
sentences.i: And when the fowler came running up, the lark said: « You there, if this is the sort of city you are founding, you will not find many to live in it. »
sentences.n: Ὦ οὗτος is the abrupt address 'you there', used to hail someone at a distance or to bring him up short — the fox uses it at fable 160 and the man at fable 60. ἐκεῖνος, 'that one', points away from the nearest subject: the speaker is the lark in the noose, not the fowler running up.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι τότε μάλιστα οἶκοι καὶ πόλεις ἐρημοῦνται, ὅταν οἱ προεστῶτες χαλεπαίνωσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti tote malista oikoi kai poleis erēmountai, hotan hoi proestōtes chalepainōsin.
sentences.l: The fable shows that houses and cities are then most of all emptied, whenever those set over them are harsh.
sentences.n: προεστῶτες is the perfect participle of προΐστημι used as a noun — 'those who have taken their stand in front', the men in charge. The correlative τότε μάλιστα … ὅταν, 'then most of all … whenever', is a favourite shape in these morals (fables 27 and 39 close the same way).
